challenges.name: context-across-emitters-and-queues
challenges.title: Where the context is lost
challenges.description: Two statements on the incident of this lesson: a scan-result log line with the antivirus poller's trace id, and a grading worker whose spans start new traces. Decide what each piece of evidence shows about where the context was captured.

questions.explanation: True. An EventEmitter keeps its listeners in a list and calls them synchronously from emit(). AsyncLocalStorage only restores a context for async work that Node itself created (promises, timers, I/O); a plain function call inherits whatever is active, here the antivirus.poll span the poller started. Registering the listener inside the request does not capture anything. The fix is to bind the listener where it is registered: context.bind(context.active(), listener). The common misconception is that AsyncLocalStorage makes every callback remember where it was created; it does so only for async resources, not for callbacks stored in a library's own data structures.

False. AsyncLocalStorage lives in the memory of one process. The only thing that reaches the worker is the job, and the stored job contains just the submission id: no traceparent, no carrier of any kind. With nothing to extract, the worker's startActiveSpan has no parent and the SDK correctly starts a new trace. The fix is to inject the active context into the job data in the producer (propagation.inject(context.active(), carrier)) and extract it in the worker (propagation.extract(ROOT_CONTEXT, job.data.otel)). The misconception is to treat "the SDK runs everywhere" as "the context flows everywhere"; across a process it flows only inside the message, unless an instrumentation for the queue library writes it there for you, which this job shows did not happen.

challenges.name: keep-trace-context-across-async
challenges.title: Keep the trace context across callbacks and the queue
challenges.description:
Since grading moved to a queue worker, the callbacks of POST /submissions on CodeDev log without a trace id (or with the trace of the antivirus poller) and the worker's "process grading" span starts a new trace. The file contains a tiny tracer and a context store: store.run(ctx, fn) makes ctx active only while fn runs synchronously, store.active() returns it (undefined when none). The store has no async tracking, so every callback that runs later sees no context, or the context of whoever calls it, unless you carry the context to it. The app code already calls your three helpers; write them:

- bind(fn): capture the context that is active when bind is called and return a function that runs fn with that context active (passing the arguments through and returning fn's result).
- inject(headers): when a context is active, set headers.traceparent to "00-<traceId>-<spanId>-01"; when none is active, leave headers unchanged.
- extract(headers): read headers.traceparent and return { traceId, spanId }, or null when the header is missing or invalid. Valid means: version "00", a 32-character and a 16-character id of lowercase hex digits, 2 hex digits of flags, separated by "-", and neither id all zeros. Any other version is invalid in this challenge.

Input (stdin): { "requests": [{ "id": "sub_101", "traceparent"?: string, "timerMs": number, "jobHeader"?: string | null }] }. The runner handles the requests one after another, then lets promises settle, fires the timers in time order, lets the antivirus poller report the scans (newest first, from its own span), and runs the worker on each job in queue order (jobHeader replaces the job's traceparent on its way through the queue; null removes it).
Output: one line per span start (span "name" trace=... span=... parent=...|none) and per log line (<id> <step>: trace=... span=... or: no context). Ids are deterministic. Do not change the store, the tracer, the app code or the test runner.
hints: A callback can only see the context that was active at some moment you saved. Which moment do you need: when bind() is called inside the request, or when the scheduler, the emitter or the promise finally calls the callback?

Look at what bind() returns and where the captured value lives. Each call to bind() needs its own captured context; with three requests in flight, a single shared variable is overwritten by the last one. For extract(), list every way a traceparent can be wrong before writing the check.

A similar case on other data: function withUser(fn) { const user = session.current(); return (...args) => session.as(user, () => fn(...args)); } saves the user when withUser runs and restores it when the returned function runs, however much later. For parsing, a header like "v1;id=abc" is safer checked with one anchored regular expression than with split(";"), which accepts too much.
